title: Audrey renonce au rôle  (Audrey Gives Up the Role)

segments.t: After comforting young Armelle Borzek over tea and giving her back the role in Augustin's film, Audrey walks out into the street with Mathias. Mathias worked hard to get her the part so she could pay her late taxes, and he is furious that she just gave it away. Let's listen to their argument in French first. Don't worry if it goes fast; you'll catch the main feelings.
Augustin avait choisi une autre actrice. C'était horrible.
Les acteurs prennent toujours le rôle d'un autre.
Tu as bien regardé Armelle? Elle va être fantastique!
Alors tu n'as pas besoin d'argent, finalement.
Tu as une vision horrible de la vie. Elle m'a touchée.
Ce n'est pas pour ça! Tu ne veux pas quitter tes enfants.
N'importe quoi!
Tes enfants vont grandir et partir.
Je veux travailler, mais ils sont petits!
Ils ont besoin de moi. Alors je fais quoi?
Je les abandonne six mois? Tu ne m'as pas parlé du Canada!
Je ne savais pas.
Et c'est impossible de travailler avec un bébé partout.
Tu dois beaucoup d'argent aux impôts.
Mais je te souhaite bonne chance!
Bonjour!
Let's go back through the argument. Audrey starts by blaming Mathias for hiding the truth.
Augustin avait choisi une autre actrice. C'était horrible.

'Augustin had chosen another actress. It was horrible.' The first action was already completed before this argument: a past helping form of 'have' comes before 'chosen'. The next sentence reacts to the encounter.
Les acteurs prennent toujours le rôle d'un autre.
'Actors always take someone else's role.' The action word 'to take' is in its plural form, and 'always' sits right after it.
Tu as bien regardé Armelle? Elle va être fantastique!
'Did you take a good look at Armelle? She's going to be fantastic!' First the past with 'have', then the near future with 'is going to be'.
Alors tu n'as pas besoin d'argent, finalement.
'So you don't need money, after all.' French says 'have need of' for 'need'. The short linking sound before money belongs to that expression; it is not an article changed by the negative.
Tu as une vision horrible de la vie. Elle m'a touchée.
'You have a horrible view of life. She moved me.' The last verb literally means 'touched', and takes a feminine ending because 'me' is Audrey.
Ce n'est pas pour ça! Tu ne veux pas quitter tes enfants.

'It's not because of that! You don't want to leave your children.' The first short phrase rejects her explanation. The second negative surrounds 'want', while 'leave' stays in its plain form afterwards.
N'importe quoi!
'Nonsense!' Audrey uses a very common three-word expression that literally means 'no matter what', used whenever someone says something ridiculous.
Tes enfants vont grandir et partir.
'Your children are going to grow up and leave.' The near future again: 'are going to' followed by two verbs.
Je veux travailler, mais ils sont petits!
'I want to work, but they're small!' The plural word for 'they' refers back to her children. The describing word for 'small' has a plural written ending to match them.
Ils ont besoin de moi. Alors je fais quoi?
'They need me. So what do I do?' There's that 'have need of' expression again, this time in the third person plural.
Je les abandonne six mois? Tu ne m'as pas parlé du Canada!
'Do I abandon them for six months? You didn't tell me about Canada!' The little word for 'them' goes before the verb. With a masculine country name like Canada, 'about' combines with 'the'.
Je ne savais pas.
'I didn't know.' This past form of 'know' describes someone's state of knowledge. It is different from saying that they found something out at a particular moment.
Et c'est impossible de travailler avec un bébé partout.

'And it's impossible to work with a baby around all the time.' The description 'impossible' is followed by a linking word and the plain action 'work'. This is Audrey's objection to taking her baby everywhere.
Tu dois beaucoup d'argent aux impôts.
'You owe a lot of money in taxes.' The action word here means 'owe'. Before another action it can mean 'must', but before an amount of money it describes a debt.
Mais je te souhaite bonne chance!

'But I wish you good luck!' Audrey turns the farewell back on Mathias. The word for 'you' comes before 'wish' and marks the person receiving the wish; the describing word for 'good' agrees with feminine 'luck'.
Bonjour!
'Hello!' Mathias has returned to the agency. The same everyday greeting works when arriving at an office as when meeting someone outside. Now let's listen to the entire dialogue once more.
Augustin avait choisi une autre actrice. C'était horrible.
Les acteurs prennent toujours le rôle d'un autre.
Tu as bien regardé Armelle? Elle va être fantastique!
Alors tu n'as pas besoin d'argent, finalement.
Tu as une vision horrible de la vie. Elle m'a touchée.
Ce n'est pas pour ça! Tu ne veux pas quitter tes enfants.
N'importe quoi!
Tes enfants vont grandir et partir.
Je veux travailler, mais ils sont petits!
Ils ont besoin de moi. Alors je fais quoi?
Je les abandonne six mois? Tu ne m'as pas parlé du Canada!
Je ne savais pas.
Et c'est impossible de travailler avec un bébé partout.
Tu dois beaucoup d'argent aux impôts.
Mais je te souhaite bonne chance!
Bonjour!

Audrey refuses to spend months away from her young children, despite the tax bill she still faces. Mathias leaves in frustration and returns to the agency. You heard how to express a need, explain an objection and remind someone about a debt. See you next time!
À bientôt!
